nodes.title: Absence — الغياب | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

«لا توسّل ينفع ولا وعيد»
English: No pleading would help, and no threat.

There is a specific kind of despair that belongs to the person who has tried everything — who has pleaded and then gone silent, who has stayed and then left, and found that neither gesture changes anything. This line does not dramatise the feeling. It simply states it. It arrived as something already known to the body, a sentence that had been true for a long time before it found its words.

A deep crimson mark cuts diagonally across a cool, scratched linen ground — less a brushstroke than a wound, or a fact. The calligraphy does not sit on top of it; it is caught inside it, cream and black ink tangled together, neither floating free nor fully grounded. The surface beneath carries the memory of texture, of something worn and reworked. The composition does not offer resolution. It holds the moment before resignation becomes peace — the exact place where absence still burns.

"بقيتُ في حضرتك رغم صمتي أقول الكثير"

nodes.title: Crossroads — تقاطع طرق | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"الدهر يعاديني وأنا ما أزال أعندْ" English: Time is against me — and I am still defiant.

This poem begins in loss and refuses to end there. She moves away — but she remains the only fate he knows. He cannot say whether he will forget her. What he can say, what he knows with absolute certainty, is that time is working against him and he has chosen, stubbornly and without apology, to resist it.

The Arabic word أعند carries something English cannot hold in a single word — it is not just defiance but the specific defiance of someone who knows they are losing and continues anyway. The fighter who will not tap out. The lover who will not let go. The poet who will not stop writing.

The composition makes that refusal visible. Broad brushstrokes in cobalt blue and deep plum collide across a crumpled paper surface — two forces that do not resolve, that do not blend into something harmonious, that simply press against each other with full weight. The script cuts through both, belonging to neither, still moving.

This is not a poem about hope. It is a poem about what you do when hope is not available.

nodes.title: Destined — مكتوب | Arabic Calligraphy Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"أنِر دربَكَ وامضِ"
English: Illuminate your path — and keep moving.

This is not a line from a poem. It is a phrase the artist wrote for himself, carried long enough that it became permanent — it lives on his shoulder now, tattooed into skin. This print is the same phrase given space on paper, surrounded by the energy that made it worth keeping.

The composition layers two registers of Arabic script: the central verse glows white against the dark, neon-like, lifted from the surface as though lit from within. Around and behind it, a second layer of calligraphy — a different phrase, its meaning kept to the artist alone. It is not hidden to create mystique. It is hidden because some words were never meant to be translated.

The background moves through rose, amber, gold, and deep magenta — raw, textured, alive. The dark border holds it all, the way a frame holds something that doesn't quite fit inside it.

nodes.title: Lebanon — لبنان | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"لبنان — حرفان في خمسة" English: Lebanon — two letters in five.

This poem arrives as reduction. Not a poem about Lebanon but a poem that performs what Lebanon does to language — compresses it, makes five letters carry more than five letters should. The arithmetic in the title is not a riddle. It is a statement about weight: that a name can mean more than it contains, that a country can live inside a person the way a word lives inside its letters.

The speaker is not describing Lebanon from the outside. He is reporting on what happens when life inside him goes still — and what moves it again. A small piece of land. Not a monument. Not a symbol. A piece of land, the way a person is a piece of something larger that cannot be named.

Within the Lebanon Collection, this piece is the one that refuses to grieve. The others hold loss, darkness, resistance. This one holds something more difficult: the stubborn, inarticulate fact of love for a place that keeps failing the people who carry it. The poem does not ask Lebanon to deserve it.

The composition makes that refusal visible. Vertical colour fields — sage, terracotta, slate blue — hold the landscape flat, stripped of its symbols. The script moves across all of them, belonging to none, crossing everything. What anchors the piece is the sweep of a line that does not stay inside the frame. Lebanon never did either.

Printed as a limited-edition fine art piece, this work is available in multiple sizes from A4 to A0. Edition sizes: A4 (15), A3 (12), A2 (10), A1 (5), A0 (3). Each print is produced on archival-quality Hahnemühle fine art paper to preserve depth, texture, and tonal nuance.

nodes.title: Prayer — صلاة | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ (Copy)
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"رهباني قدّسوا في السماء شياطينك"

English: My monks have hallowed in heaven your demons.

This poem arrives dressed as devotion and reveals itself as desire. The speaker's monks do not pray to God — they pray to the beloved, sanctifying even her demons, finding the sacred inside what should be transgressive. The final lines collapse the distance between prayer and longing entirely: her image appears not in dreams but during the recitation of her own name as prayer.

Within the Lebanon Collection, this piece occupies a specific place: Lebanon too is loved this way — with full knowledge of its darkness, with monks who have long since redirected their prayers toward something that does not deserve them and cannot stop receiving them.

The composition makes visible what Arabic reading usually moves past without seeing: the diacritical points — the small marks that distinguish letters, that carry meaning, that most eyes skip over — are pulled from the script and rendered as solid gold geometric forms beneath it. What anchors the piece is not decoration but punctuation. The smallest unit of linguistic meaning becomes the largest visual presence. The script floats above what it depends on.

nodes.title: Resistance - مقاومة | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ (Copy)
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"سَأَقْلِبُ السُّكُونَ في كَلامِكِ ضَمَّة"

English: I will turn the silence in your words into an embrace.

This work is taken from a poem of resistance — not against a person, but against surrender itself. The speaker refuses the posture of the wounded, refuses to accept absence as a final condition, and instead imagines storming every fortress of the beloved, gathering an army of all those undone by a single glance. The resistance is not to push her away. It is to make her return.

The composition holds that tension visibly. Two forces — black and gold — move through each other without resolution, neither consuming the other. The parchment ground carries the texture of something written and rewritten, layered with the pressure of words that refused to stay silent. The flashes of red embedded in the dark forms are not decorative. They are the cost of not surrendering.

nodes.title: Text Message — غيرِك | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

«غيرِك»
English: Anyone but you.

This piece begins where a poem ends. A text message written in Lebanese Arabic — the kind that arrives at an ordinary hour and says something that cannot be unsaid. By the end of it, one line holds everything: the eyes, the problem is, don't see anyone but you. The word is not a declaration. It is a diagnosis. The person writing it has noticed something about themselves — that the world has quietly rearranged itself around one person, without asking.

The calligraphy opens outward, heavy at the centre and dissolving at the edges, as if the word is still being released. Orange marks interrupt the black — not decoration, but punctuation that insists. Beneath the main script, a ghost of the same word turns in the linen ground — echo, or memory, or the thought before it became language. The composition has the feeling of something said too loudly in a quiet room.

nodes.title: The Cedar — الأرزة | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"ما زلت هنا — ومازال حبك رغم كل شيء يعنيني" English: I am still here — and your love, despite everything, still matters to me.

This poem is structured like a day. It begins with a morning instruction the speaker gives himself — forget her, she has forgotten you. It does not work. He lives the day anyway, with her ghost and the wounds, and by evening his defenses have collapsed and only one thing is still standing: loyalty. Not to her. To what he said. To what he promised. To the stubborn heart that still means what it meant.

The Arabic word يعنيني is doing everything in the final verse. It does not mean love — it means matters, concerns, is meaningful to. It is quieter than love and more honest. After a full day of trying to forget, after the evening defeat, what he sends from his silent phone is not a declaration. It is a confession of relevance. You still matter. That is all. That is everything.

The Cedar is the national symbol of Lebanon — the tree that does not break, that survives altitude and storm, that remains. The title is not decorative. This poem is about the same endurance: not passion that burns, but the kind that simply does not stop being true.

The composition holds all of that colour and noise — the full spectrum of the day, teal to coral to gold — beneath a Kufic geometric pattern that runs like a labyrinth through the entire surface. The script cuts through it in black, certain and large, as though the maze were always just background and the words were always the only thing that mattered.

nodes.title: The Oracle — العرّافة | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"انصهري بلورةً سحريةً لا تنطفئ متى بردت" English: Melt into a magic crystal — one that does not go out when it grows cold.

This poem begins with a tear that cannot decide whether to fall. What follows is one of the most sustained acts of surrender in the Arabic language — not the surrender of defeat but the surrender of someone who has tried control and found it useless. The speaker stops directing. He lets the tear go where it wants. He lets it travel, water dry earth, wet pages that have gone stiff in notebooks he no longer opens. He lets it decide.

And then the reversal. The tear does not want to decide. It has found something better to do than fall — it has taken up residence in the eyelid and grown comfortable there, doing its quiet work on the person who carries it.

The verse the composition carries is the hinge of the whole poem: انصهري بلورةً سحريةً لا تنطفئ متى بردت. Melt into a magic crystal that does not go out when it grows cold. This is not a prayer. It is an instruction — given to a tear, to a love, to something the speaker cannot name directly but addresses as though it can hear him.

The composition gives that instruction its form. Teal sweeps across linen like a tide that has not yet decided to recede. Acid green holds the lower edge, alive and unsettled. At the centre, barely visible, a moon — the traditional witness of Arabic poetry, the thing that does not go out when it grows cold. The script descends through all of it, tightening as it falls, the way a voice does when it says something it means completely.

nodes.title: The Sculptor — النحّات | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

«كَتِمْثالٍ صُبَّ عَلى جَمَد»
English: Like a statue cast over ice.

There is a kind of composure that is not peace — that is damage made presentable. This line comes from a poem of return: come back, it says, I won't ask for anything. I won't mention what is stirring. I will give back every loss you left with me. I will be cold. The coldness here is not indifference. It is what the person has decided to become — a statue, a thing shaped and hardened and fixed, poured over ice so that it holds its form no matter what comes next.

The calligraphy descends the page in a vertical cascade, as if it is itself being poured — heavy, unhurried, black ink on bare linen. Beside it, a deep teal wash cuts through the composition: cold, waterlogged, dissolving at the edges. The two halves do not meet cleanly. At the base, rust-coloured leaves have settled — the poem's closing image made visible, a garden whose wounds dried up and no longer water the roses. The composition is divided, and stays divided.

As a triptych, this work unfolds across three registers — three moments, three perspectives, or three stages of the same experience. Each section is complete in itself while remaining part of a larger whole. The script moves differently across each panel, reflecting the shifting nature of what is being described.

nodes.title: The Warrior — المحارب | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"ثم أعود معلناً الحرب ولاعناً السلام"

English: Then I return, declaring war and cursing peace.

This piece comes from a poem about the particular stubbornness of someone who keeps surrendering and keeps coming back. The white flag is burned — not in triumph, but in exhaustion with surrender itself. The speaker does not return because he is strong. He returns because he cannot stop.

The form is a faceted geometric solid — a shield, a stone, a medallion — something that has absorbed impact and holds its shape anyway. The patina green surface carries the texture of oxidised metal, of things left in weather for a long time. The copper-rose edges and the gold dust swept across the ground are not decoration. They are what remains after a long war with oneself.

The script sits inside the form like something engraved — not written on the surface but pressed into it. The verse is not a caption. It is the object itself.

nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

"تخرجين من قلبي الهوينة/ لساعات وبمجهودٍ لأيامِ/ ثم أعود حارقاً رايتي البيضاء/ معلناً الحرب ولاعناً /السلام"

English: You leave my heart slowly, for hours, and with effort, for days — then I return burning my white flag, declaring war and cursing peace.

This work explores the same emotional territory as The Dark Knight, rendered in its opposite register — the surrender rather than the revolt, the white flag before it burns.

Where The Dark Knight holds tension and weight, The White Knight offers space and breath. The composition is lighter in tone but no less serious in intention — this is the version of the poem that precedes the war, when peace still felt possible.

nodes.title: Vision — رؤيا | Arabic Poetry Art Print | ENJZ
nodes.descriptionHtml:
Original giclée on Hahnemühle archival paper. Signed and numbered by the artist.

رؤية — Vision "إلى اليوم ما زلت رغم البعد مفتون" "To this day, I remain — despite the distance — enchanted."

Some distances never close. They only deepen.

Vision is a confession that time and geography cannot cure — the kind of longing that doesn't diminish with years but settles into the body, becoming part of how you carry yourself through the world.

The central form — dense, interlocking, almost sculptural — renders the word مفتون (enchanted, captivated, spellbound) as something that cannot be untangled. The letters spiral inward and outward simultaneously, the way obsession does. Gold leaf fractures across the surface, suggesting something precious that has weathered — not broken, but burnished by endurance.

Above the form, three ghosted lines drift like half-remembered breath: إلى اليوم — ما زلت — رغم البعد. They rise into the blue like smoke, barely there, the way a verse lives in your throat long after the moment has passed.

The ground moves from deep cobalt through teal, sun-yellow, blush, and into burning red — a full arc of feeling, a whole sky compressed into a single field. This is not decoration. It is the emotional temperature of the poem made visible.
